input: whats the small cache on the cpu that stores recent address translations?
expected_output: It is the TLB (translation-lookaside buffer). It is part of the chip's memory-management unit and is a hardware cache of popular virtual-to-physical address translations, which is why a better name would be an address-translation cache.

evidence.quote: A TLB is part of the chip’s memory-management unit (MMU), and is simply a hardware cache of popular virtual-to-physical address translations; thus, a better name would be an address-translation cache.

input: what do the two kinds of locality mean and why do caches depend on them?
expected_output: Temporal locality means something accessed recently will probably be accessed again soon, like loop variables or instructions in a loop. Spatial locality means that if a program touches address x it will likely touch nearby memory soon, like walking through an array. Caches exploit both by keeping copies of memory in small, fast on-chip memory.

evidence.quote: With temporal locality, the idea is that an instruction or data item that has been recently accessed will likely be re-accessed soon in the future.
With spatial locality, the idea is that if a program accesses memory at address x, it will likely soon access memory near x.
Hardware caches, whether for instructions, data, or address translations (as in our TLB) take advantage of locality by keeping copies of memory in small, fast on-chip memory.
Think of loop variables or instructions in a loop; they are accessed repeatedly over time.
Imagine here streaming through an array of some kind, accessing one element and then the next.

input: if the tlb gets wiped whenever the cpu changes to a different process, what's the downside?
expected_output: Wiping the TLB gives a correct solution, since a process can never pick up the wrong translations. The cost is that each time a process runs it has to take TLB misses as it touches its data and code pages, so if the OS switches between processes frequently this cost can be high.

evidence.quote: By flushing the TLB on each context switch, we now have a working solution, as a process will never accidentally encounter the wrong translations in the TLB. However, there is a cost: each time a process runs, it must incur TLB misses as it touches its data and code pages.
If the OS switches between processes frequently, this cost may be high.

input: how does the tlb keep entries from different programs apart? is it some id field
expected_output: Some hardware adds an address space identifier (ASID) field to each TLB entry. It works like a process ID but with fewer bits. Two entries with the same virtual page number can then be told apart just by their ASID, so translations from different processes can sit in the TLB together without confusion.

evidence.quote: You can think of the ASID as a process identifier (PID), but usually it has fewer bits (e.g., 8 bits for the ASID versus 32 bits for a PID).
If we take our example TLB from above and add ASIDs, it is clear processes can readily share the TLB: only the ASID field is needed to differentiate otherwise identical translations.
Thus, with address-space identifiers, the TLB can hold translations from different processes at the same time without any confusion.
In particular, some hardware systems provide an address space identifier (ASID) field in the TLB.

input: why does the cpu rerun the same instruction after a tlb miss, not the next one
expected_output: Because the instruction that caused the miss never finished. After the handler loads the translation, the hardware must resume at the instruction that trapped so it runs again, and this time it results in a TLB hit. So the hardware has to save a different PC depending on whether the trap was caused by something like a TLB miss or by another kind of trap.

evidence.quote: In the former case, when returning from a TLB miss-handling trap, the hardware must resume execution at the instruction that caused the trap; this retry thus lets the instruction run again, this time resulting in a TLB hit.
Thus, depending on how a trap or exception was caused, the hardware must save a different PC when trapping into the OS, in order to resume properly when the time to do so arrives.

input: why can't they just build a giant tlb so everything always fits?
expected_output: A fast cache has to be small because physical constraints like the speed of light come into play. Any large cache is by definition slow, which defeats the purpose of having it, so designers are stuck with small, fast caches.

evidence.quote: If you want a fast cache, it has to be small, as issues like the speed-of-light and other physical constraints become relevant. Any large cache by definition is slow, and thus defeats the purpose.

input: How does handling a missed translation differ between older x86-style CPUs and MIPS or SPARC style CPUs, and what is the benefit of the newer approach?
expected_output: On the older x86-style design the hardware handles the miss itself: it walks the page table, finds the entry, updates the TLB, and retries the instruction. On MIPS/SPARC-style chips the hardware just raises an exception that traps into OS code (a handler), which does the lookup. The benefit of the OS-handled approach is flexibility, since the OS can use any page-table data structure without a hardware change.

evidence.quote: on a miss, the hardware would “walk” the page table, find the correct page-table entry and extract the desired translation, update the TLB with the translation, and retry the instruction.
On a TLB miss, the hardware simply raises an exception (line 11 in Figure 19.3), which pauses the current instruction stream, raises the privilege level to kernel mode, and jumps to a trap handler.
The primary advantage of the software-managed approach is flexibility: the OS can use any data structure it wants to implement the page table, without necessitating hardware change.

An example of an “older” architecture that has hardware-managed TLBs is the Intel x86 architecture, which uses a fixed multi-level page table (see the next chapter for details); the current page table is pointed to by the CR3 register [I09].
More modern architectures (e.g., MIPS R10k [H93] or Sun’s SPARC v9 [WG00], both RISC or reduced-instruction set computers) have what is known as a software-managed TLB.

When run, the code will lookup the translation in the page table, use special “privileged” instructions to update the TLB, and return from the trap; at this point, the hardware retries the instruction (resulting in a TLB hit).

input: is the valid bit on a tlb entry the same as the one on a pte? kinda confused
expected_output: No, they mean different things. A page-table entry marked invalid means the process never allocated that page and should not touch it, and accessing it usually traps to the OS, which kills the process. A TLB valid bit only says whether that TLB entry currently holds a valid translation.

evidence.quote: In a page table, when a page-table entry (PTE) is marked invalid, it means that the page has not been allocated by the process, and should not be accessed by a correctly-working program.
A TLB valid bit, in contrast, simply refers to whether a TLB entry has a valid translation within it.
The usual response when an invalid page is accessed is to trap to the OS, which will respond by killing the process.

input: say i loop once over 12 ints, 4 bytes each, 16 byte pages, array starts at a page boundary and tlb is empty. hit rate?
expected_output: Each 16-byte page holds 4 of the 4-byte ints, so the array spans 3 pages. Only the first access to an element on each page misses, giving 3 misses and 9 hits out of 12 accesses. Hit rate is hits divided by total accesses, so 9/12 = 75%.

evidence.quote: The elements of the array are packed tightly into pages (i.e., they are close to one another in space), and thus only the first access to an element on a page yields a TLB miss.

input: mips has some special tlb instructions, what do they do and why cant user programs run them
expected_output: MIPS has four: TLBP probes the TLB for a particular translation, TLBR reads a TLB entry into registers, TLBWI replaces a specific entry, and TLBWR replaces a random entry. They must be privileged, because a user process that could modify the TLB could do just about anything, including taking over the machine.

evidence.quote: The MIPS provides four such instructions: TLBP, which probes the TLB to see if a particular translation is in there; TLBR, which reads the contents of a TLB entry into registers; TLBWI, which replaces a specific TLB entry; and TLBWR, which replaces a random TLB entry.

It is of course critical that these instructions are privileged; imagine what a user process could do if it could modify the contents of the TLB (hint: just about anything, including take over the machine, run its own malicious “OS”, or even make the Sun disappear).

input: ram is random access so why is jumping around a huge array slower than going in order?
expected_output: Treating RAM as uniform is usually fine, but it is not always true. Because of features like the TLB, accessing a page can be costly if that page isn't currently mapped by the TLB. Randomly accessing an address space, especially touching more pages than the TLB covers, can cause severe performance penalties.

evidence.quote: While it is generally good to think of RAM in this way, because of hardware/OS features such as the TLB, accessing a particular page of memory may be costly, particularly if that page isn’t currently mapped by your TLB.
Sometimes randomly accessing your address space, particular if the number of pages accessed exceeds the TLB coverage, can lead to severe performance penalties.

input: why does my big database slow down alot when it jumps arround tons of memory
expected_output: If a program touches more pages in a short time than fit in the TLB (exceeding the TLB coverage), it generates many TLB misses and runs noticeably slower.

evidence.quote: if the number of pages a program accesses in a short period of time exceeds the number of pages that fit into the TLB, the program will generate a large number of TLB misses, and thus run quite a bit more slowly.
We refer to this phenomenon as exceeding the TLB coverage, and it can be quite a problem for certain programs.
